# Run it as a systemd service

> Install the binary and a hardened unit, keep it enabled across reboots, and upgrade or roll back without losing the paths it needs.

## Install

A release ships a checksum-verified tarball; the installer also accepts a build
you made yourself, which is what you want before the first release exists:

```bash
# from the published release
sudo sh packaging/install.sh --workspace /srv/karucode/workspace

# from a local build
cargo build --release -p kc-server
sudo sh packaging/install.sh --binary target/release/karucode \
     --workspace /srv/karucode/workspace

# preview first, change nothing
sudo sh packaging/install.sh --workspace /srv/karucode/workspace --dry-run
```

A prebuilt release archive can be installed with `sudo sh packaging/install.sh
--tarball /path/to/release.tar.gz --workspace /srv/karucode/workspace`. If a
sibling `SHA256SUMS` exists, it must contain the archive's basename and matching
SHA-256; an absent entry is an error, not permission to install without
verification. With no sibling checksum file the local-archive behavior is
unchanged. Use `--binary` for a locally compiled executable instead.

`--workspace` is the one directory the agent may read and edit. The installer
creates it, owns it by the service user, installs the unit, enables it at boot,
starts it, and only reports success once `/api/health` answers. It writes a
commented template to `/etc/karucode/karucode.env` only when that file does not
exist.

**The service runs as the account that ran the installer.** There is no
dedicated `karucode` account to create and no `--service-user` to pass: a plain
`sudo sh install.sh` from your account resolves to *you*, because the agent is
useless if it cannot reach your toolchains, `~/.cargo`, `~/.local/bin` or your
projects. The installer resolves the account from `$SUDO_USER`, then `$LOGNAME`,
then the session login uid, and treats `$USER` as evidence only when it is not
`root` (under `sudo` it always is). Root is refused in every spelling —
`--service-user root`, `0`, `00`, `root:root` and `0:0` all exit 1. The account
is never created and its files are never re-owned; `--service-user` names an
*existing* account and refuses one that does not exist.

The data directory follows the account: `~/.local/share/karucode` for a person,
the account's own home for a system account (`--service-user karucode` gives
`/var/lib/karucode`, not `/var/lib/karucode/.local/share/karucode`). The group
comes from the account's real primary gid rather than from an assumption that
`name == group`; `--service-group` overrides it.

When no human can be identified at all — a bare `sudo -i` shell or a container
build, where `$SUDO_USER`, `$LOGNAME` and the login uid all say root — the
installer falls back to the `karucode` system account, creating it if missing,
and **says so loudly**. Both the per-step output and the final summary name the
resolved account (`Service account: user:group`), so `systemctl show -p User -p
Group karucode` can be checked against what the install reported instead of
assumed.

Exit codes: `0` installed and running, `1` nothing installed (or rolled back),
`2` installed but the service did not come up — then it prints the four things
worth checking (busy port, workspace permissions, data-dir permissions, a bad
value in the env file).

## The paths live in a drop-in, not in the unit

```
/etc/systemd/system/karucode.service              shipped, replaced on upgrade
/etc/systemd/system/karucode.service.d/
    10-install.conf                              generated, rewritten on upgrade
    20-local.conf                                yours, never touched
```

`WorkingDirectory=`, `User=`, the port and `ExecStart=` are written to
`10-install.conf`. Editing the unit in place does not stick: the next
install replaces the file, and the service then fails with `status=200/CHDIR`
because the workspace path it needs is gone. Put local overrides in
`20-local.conf` and `sudo systemctl daemon-reload` afterwards — the filename must
end in `.conf` or systemd ignores it.

```ini
# /etc/systemd/system/karucode.service.d/20-local.conf
[Service]
Environment=PATH=/home/you/.cargo/bin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin
MemoryDenyWriteExecute=no
```

## Concurrency with other toolchains

The service gets systemd's default `PATH`, not your shell's, so `cargo`, `pnpm`,
`bun` and an `nvm`-managed `node` are not found by the agent's shell. Set
`Environment=PATH=…` in `20-local.conf`. `MemoryDenyWriteExecute=yes` in the
unit also stops `node`, Java and some Python C extensions; `install.sh
--allow-jit` turns it off, or set it to `no` yourself.

The unit does **not** sandbox the filesystem: the agent can write anywhere the
service user can, so `mv`/`cp`/`rm` work across the filesystem and no build
fails with `EROFS`. Confinement is the dedicated unprivileged `User=` plus
`NoNewPrivileges=yes`. If you want a filesystem sandbox, add `ProtectSystem=`,
`ProtectHome=` and `ReadWritePaths=` yourself in `20-local.conf` — the shipped
unit leaves those out on purpose. See `packaging/README.md`.

## Credentials

The unit reads `/etc/karucode/karucode.env` (mode 0600, owned by root) after its
own `Environment=` lines, so the file wins. Set at least the model connection,
then restart:

```sh
KARUCODE_BASE_URL=https://api.example.com/v1
KARUCODE_API_KEY=sk-...
KARUCODE_MODEL=gpt-4o-mini
KARUCODE_AUTH_TOKEN=<32+ random chars>   # openssl rand -hex 32
KARUCODE_ADMIN_TOKEN=<32+ random chars>
```

```bash
sudo systemctl restart karucode && journalctl -u karucode -f
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $KARUCODE_AUTH_TOKEN" localhost:8787/api/health
```

Without a token the loopback bind is still safe: the server only answers for
`Host: 127.0.0.1`, `localhost` or `[::1]`. A non-loopback bind refuses to start
without `KARUCODE_AUTH_TOKEN`. The binary has no TLS — terminate it in a reverse
proxy.

## Upgrade, roll back, remove

Re-running the installer is the upgrade: it verifies the new tarball, replaces
the binary, rewrites the unit and the drop-in, and restarts a running service
onto the new binary (so the old process is not left serving). The previous
binary stays at `/usr/local/bin/karucode.old`, the previous unit at
`karucode.service.bak`, and the env file, the database and `20-local.conf` are
untouched.

```bash
sudo sh packaging/install.sh --version 107 --workspace /srv/karucode/workspace
sudo cp -p /usr/local/bin/karucode.old /usr/local/bin/karucode   # roll back
sudo systemctl restart karucode
```

`--version` is a release to fetch, and a release is a build number: every
commit on `main` is released as `v<commit count>` (build 107 is the 107th
commit). There is no semver to bump - `karucode --version` and the tarball name
both carry the same integer.

## Updating an installed release

A binary installed by `install.sh` updates itself from the release manifest
(`updates.json`, published beside every tarball):

```bash
karucode update --check        # 0 up to date, 3 a newer build exists, 1 error
sudo karucode update --apply --data-dir /var/lib/karucode
sudo karucode update --apply --data-dir /var/lib/karucode --restart
```

The service account usually cannot write `/usr/local/bin/karucode`, so the
server stages and *verifies* the download (checksum, size, and the artifact's
own `--version`) and **Settings → Updates** prints exactly the command above;
`--apply` is the only step that needs root, and it keeps the old binary as
`karucode.old`. `--restart` runs `systemctl restart karucode` afterwards
(`KARUCODE_SERVICE` names another unit); without it the new build is installed
and the running process keeps serving the old one until you restart.

The server checks the manifest on startup and every six hours by default and
raises a notification when a newer build exists. `[updates]` decides that:

```toml
[updates]
check = true                 # KARUCODE_UPDATE_CHECK=0 turns it off entirely
check_secs = 21600           # 300..=604800
manifest_url = "https://github.com/karutoil/karucode/releases/latest/download/updates.json"
auto_apply = false           # never install without a click
```

Point `manifest_url` at a mirror you control if you do not want to fetch from
GitHub; the manifest is the trust anchor for what gets installed. `[updates]`
is in the `configuration` topic and the whole procedure - the manifest format,
the staging directory, the privilege boundary - is the `updates` topic. A
container install refuses all of this: rebuild the image.

## Updating from your own build

If the service runs a binary you compiled yourself, `packaging/update.sh` is
the one command: it pulls, builds, stages, snapshots the database and installs.

```bash
sudo sh packaging/update.sh              # pull, build, stage, install, restart
sh packaging/update.sh --check           # exit 3 if commits are waiting
sudo sh packaging/update.sh --dry-run    # print the plan, change nothing
```

It does not reimplement the systemd half — it reads the *running* unit
(`ExecStart=`, `User=`, `WorkingDirectory=`, `KARUCODE_*`, and
`MemoryDenyWriteExecute=`, which becomes `--allow-jit`) and hands that
configuration to `install.sh`, so the paths the service actually starts with
survive. The defaults compiled into `install.sh` are for a fresh host and
would otherwise replace them on the first update.

### Staged, then switched

Everything that can fail happens before anything live is touched. The binary
and the unit are copied into a stage directory and *those copies* are
validated — the binary has to run, the unit has to parse, and a sha256 of the
staged binary is recorded. Only then does the switch move the binary, rewrite
the drop-in and restart the unit. A build that produces a binary for the wrong
libc, or a truncated download, is therefore caught while the old binary is
still serving.

```bash
sudo sh packaging/update.sh --stage-only   # build and validate; stop there
sudo sh packaging/update.sh --from-stage   # switch onto it; no rebuild
```

`--stage-only` is the maintenance-window form: it reports the staged version
and sha256 and changes nothing live. `--from-stage` applies exactly those
bytes, refuses if the staged binary no longer matches its recorded checksum,
and leaves no stage behind afterwards. It does not build or require the
original `target/release/karucode`; that file may be deleted after staging.
The stage lives in
`<data-dir>/stage` (`--stage-dir` to move it) and is root-owned, because the
build runs as you and `install.sh` reads it as root.

### Surviving the terminal

A run that builds or switches detaches itself into its own session with its
own log before doing anything, so closing the terminal — or losing the SSH
connection — cannot stop an update half way through the switch.

```bash
sh packaging/update.sh --follow            # reattach to the last run's log
sudo sh packaging/update.sh --no-detach    # stay in the foreground
```

The job directory is `<data-dir>/update-job`: `log`, `pid` and, when it
finishes, `status` (the exit code). The waiting shell forwards that code, so
`sudo sh packaging/update.sh` still exits `0`, `1` or `2` as documented.
Detaching is skipped when there is no terminal (a `sudo` password prompt
could not be answered), for `--check`, `--dry-run`, `--build-only` and
`--stage-only`, and when sudo would need to ask for a password. Two updates
cannot run at once: a lock beside the data directory refuses the second.

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `--stage-only` | Build and validate, then stop before touching the service |
| `--from-stage` | Switch onto what `--stage-only` staged; no rebuild |
| `--no-stage` | Install straight from the build, skipping the stage |
| `--detach` / `--no-detach` | Force or forbid running in the background |
| `--follow` | Attach to a detached run's log |
| `--no-pull` | build the working tree as it is (offline, or a local branch) |
| `--ref <REF>` | build a tag instead of the current branch (detached HEAD) |
| `--build-only` | compile and stop; the service is not touched |
| `--skip-build` | install the binary already in `target/release` |
| `--allow-dirty` | permit modified tracked files (refused by default) |
| `--no-backup` | skip the `VACUUM INTO` snapshot taken before the install |
| `--force` | reinstall even when the binary and unit are unchanged |

Exit codes: `0` updated and serving, `1` nothing changed (dirty tree, build
failure, no unit), `2` installed but the service did not come back, `3`
`--check` found commits you do not have. Only the stage, the snapshot and
`install.sh` run under `sudo`; the fetch and the build run as the checkout's
owner, so `target/` is not left root-owned. Run it from a normal login shell:
inside the service itself `NoNewPrivileges=yes` makes `sudo` impossible, and
the script says so instead of failing obscurely.

There is no uninstall verb; `packaging/README.md` lists the six commands
(`systemctl disable --now`, remove the unit, the drop-in, both binaries,
`daemon-reload`), plus the optional removal of `/var/lib/karucode` and
`/etc/karucode`. The database holds sessions **and the provider API key**, so
removing it is a separate decision.

## Gotchas that bite on a real host

* Running the unit inside an **unprivileged container** fails with
  `status=217/USER` or `ProtectHostname=yes is configured, but UTS namespace
  setup is prohibited`: the namespace sandboxing needs `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`. Use the
  `Dockerfile` in a container instead of this unit.
* A hand-started `karucode` on the same port makes the unit exit at startup. The
  installer warns about it before writing the unit; `ss -ltnp | grep :8787`
  finds the process.
* `MemoryDenyWriteExecute=yes` (in the unit) stops the agent from running
  `node`, Java or Python C extensions. Re-run the installer with `--allow-jit`
  rather than hand-editing the unit.
* After a failure the unit can be held by `StartLimitBurst=5`
  (`start of the service was attempted too often`); the installer clears that
  with `systemctl reset-failed` before it starts or restarts.
* `Type=simple` means systemd reports `active` the moment the process forks, so
  a service that dies 200 ms later still looks started for a moment. Health is
  `/api/health`, not `is-active`.
* The service gets the **default** `PATH` (`/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/
  usr/sbin:/usr/bin`), not your shell's. `cargo` in `~/.cargo/bin`, `pnpm`, `bun`
  and the nvm `node` are then not found by the agent's shell. Put
  `Environment=PATH=…` in `20-local.conf`.
* `MemoryDenyWriteExecute=yes` stops the agent running `node`, Java or Python C
  extensions. Re-run the installer with `--allow-jit`, or set it to `no` in
  `20-local.conf`.
* To keep an instance you already ran by hand, pass `--data-dir
  ~/.local/share/karucode`: the provider API key and every setting live in the
  database, so a fresh data directory is an empty instance, not an upgrade. The
  service account is already you, so no `--service-user` is needed.
* `sudo sh install.sh` from a *bare root shell* (`sudo -i`, a container build)
  has no human to resolve. It prints a warning and falls back to the `karucode`
  system account with `/var/lib/karucode` as the data dir. Run it as yourself,
  or pass `--service-user <name>`, if you wanted the default.

The full operator guide — reverse proxy, backups, container deployment, the
hardening rationale — is `packaging/README.md`.
